subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Lapsang Souchong: Smoked Tea
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Lapsang Souchong: Smoked Tea.

hook.text: Lapsang Souchong is tea dried over burning pinewood. It smells like a campfire in a cup.

buildup.text: Legend says soldiers camped in a tea factory, delaying production. Workers rushed drying over pine fires.

discovery.text: The smoke from Masson pine infuses the leaves with compounds called guaiacol and syringol—the flavor of smoke.

twist.text: Winston Churchill was reportedly a Lapsang fan. Some say it reminds drinkers of whisky without the alcohol.

climax.text: Original Lapsang Souchong from Wuyi Mountains is rare. Most commercial versions use artificial smoke flavor.

punchline.text: Pine smoke, bold leaves, a flavor that divides every room.

quiz.question: How is authentic Lapsang Souchong made?

details.summary: Lapsang Souchong is a black tea from Wuyi Mountain in Fujian that is smoke-dried over pine-wood fires, giving it a distinctive campfire aroma. It was historically the first black tea exported to Europe and remains polarizing: people either love or hate its intensely smoky character.
details.whyItMatters: Lapsang Souchong is a living piece of tea history, representing the moment black tea entered Western awareness and changed global tea culture forever.
takeaways: Leaves are smoke-dried over smoldering pine wood
It was the first black tea exported to Western markets
The intense smoky flavor is highly polarizing

faq.question: Why was Lapsang Souchong originally smoked?
faq.answer: Legend says farmers in Wuyi had to speed-dry their tea over pine fires when an army camped in their factory. The smoky tea sold unexpectedly well to Dutch traders. Modern non-smoked versions called Zhengshan Xiaozhong show the tea's natural sweetness without smoke.

faq.question: How should Lapsang Souchong be brewed?
faq.answer: Use boiling water at 100 degrees Celsius and steep for three to five minutes. It pairs well with savory foods, cheese, and dark chocolate. Some enjoy it with a splash of milk. For a lighter smoky note, reduce the leaf amount or steep time.
